sentences.text: The call came on a Tuesday evening in Lima, and Amaru's father was standing by the sink washing dishes when the phone rang.
He picked it up.
He listened for a long moment.
He set the plate he was drying carefully on the counter.
He said, in Quechua, three words that Amaru did not understand.
Then he sat down at the kitchen table.
Amaru knew, before his father hung up, that his great-grandfather Silverio had died.
He did not know how he knew.
He knew from his father's back.
His father had been quiet for a long time, and then he had put down the phone, and he had said, in Spanish, "Amaru.
Tayta Silverio has died." Amaru sat down at the table too.
He had met his great-grandfather only twice in his life — once when Amaru was four, once when he was seven — but he remembered both visits very clearly.
Silverio had been a tall thin man with white hair and eyes the color of good coffee, and he had a way of looking at Amaru that made Amaru feel he was being seen carefully, all the way through.
"The funeral is Saturday," his father said, later that evening.
He had spread a paper map on the kitchen table.
"I want to go.
He was my grandfather.
I want to be there." He looked at Amaru.
"I want you to come with me.
But it will not be easy.
The village is very remote.
Two years ago there was a big landslide on the road from Cusco.
The government has never rebuilt it.
To get to the village now, you have to walk.
Over the pass.
Three days."
He traced the route with his finger.
It went up from the highway, over a mountain pass at almost fifteen thousand feet, and down again into a valley on the other side.
A tiny name was written on the far side: Choquepata.
That was the village.
"The village where I grew up," his father said.
"Where I lived until I was seventeen.
Where my father lived, and his father, and his father.
Where you have never been."
"Can I do it," said Amaru.
"The walking." His father looked at him for a long moment.
"You are twelve.
You are strong.
But you have grown up in Lima at sea level.
The pass is very high.
You will feel it.
It will be hard.
You may need to stop often.
If you cannot make it, we will turn around.
That is fine.
But I think you can make it.
I think you should try." He paused.
"I think Tayta Silverio would want you to see the village.
Once, at least.
Even if only once."
So Amaru said yes.
His mother packed for him.

His father took his old backpack down from the top of the closet — the one Amaru had not seen for many years, faded green canvas with worn leather straps — and packed it with dried food and a small stove and two heavy wool blankets and a small trowel and a first aid kit and coca leaves.
On Wednesday morning they flew to Cusco.
On Thursday morning at dawn, they got out of a shared taxi at a bend in a dirt road above a river, and there was no road ahead of them, only a narrow stone path going up into the mountains.
"Ready," said his father.
Amaru nodded.
He was cold and his stomach was tight with nerves.
He shouldered his own smaller pack.
It had food and clothes and his own blanket in it.
His father's pack was much heavier.
They started walking.
The path was narrow — one person wide — and it climbed steadily.
There were no signs.
There were no other people.
There were, sometimes, small piles of stones stacked at the corners of the path, which his father said were called apachetas.
They were made by people who had walked this way before, over hundreds of years, one stone each.
His father added a stone to the first one they came to.
He said, "You do that.
Every time we pass one.
It brings you safely through."
So Amaru did.
He added a small flat grey stone to the pile.
He said, quietly, "For safe walking." And they went on.
The first day was hard but not too hard.
They climbed steadily.
Amaru got out of breath easily but he did not have to stop for long.
They ate small pieces of dried alpaca meat and hard bread as they walked.
They drank water.
His father chewed coca leaves and offered some to Amaru, who chewed them too, though he did not really like the taste.
It kept the headache away, his father said.
That was the important thing.
They stopped at midafternoon at a flat spot where there was a small stone shelter — three walls and a roof, no door.
Someone had built it long ago as a rest for travelers.
There was old dry grass in one corner for a bed.
There was a fire pit at the front.
Amaru sat down and did not want to move again for the rest of his life.
His father laughed.
"Yes," he said.
"Rest.
You did well today.
Tomorrow is the hard day.
Tomorrow we cross the pass."
